lead: A coil wound on an iron core stores magnetic energy. Its inductance depends on how easily flux crosses the magnetic path. Put a movable iron armature across a small air gap, and the gap reluctance controls the inductance. A tiny movement changes the gap, so the coil inductance changes. This is the variable reluctance transducer. It measures displacement, thickness and pressure, and is read with AC excitation, because only a changing current turns the inductance into a voltage that a bridge can measure. Two coils can also be coupled so that movement changes mutual inductance.
prereq: You need: sensitivity, linearity and calibration from the static characteristics of sensors; basic magnetic circuits (reluctance and Faraday’s law) from physics.

blocks.text: Self inductance L is the flux linkage per ampere in one coil. For a coil of N turns on a magnetic circuit of reluctance R, L = N²/R. Reluctance R is the magnetic resistance: R = l/(μ A), where l is path length in metres, A is cross-sectional area in square metres, and μ is permeability in henries per metre (H/m). Iron has large μ; air has μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.

blocks.where: L is self inductance in henries (H); N is the number of turns (no unit); R is the reluctance of the magnetic path in ampere-turns per weber (A·t/Wb) or H⁻¹.
g is air-gap length in metres; μ₀ is free-space permeability = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m; A is the gap area in square metres.

blocks.text: An iron core with a coil and a movable armature has a narrow air gap g. The total reluctance is the iron reluctance plus the gap reluctance. Iron μ is hundreds or thousands of times μ₀, so the gap usually dominates. Then R ≈ g/(μ₀ A), and L ≈ μ₀ A N² / g. Movement of the armature changes g, so L changes. This is the single-coil, or self-inductance, variable reluctance transducer.

items: Construction: a laminated iron core, one coil, a movable iron armature, and a small air gap.
Operation: energise the coil with AC; the current sets flux; the gap sets reluctance; L follows.
Read-out: put the coil in an AC bridge; armature movement unbalances the bridge.

blocks.text: A second coil can be placed on the same magnetic path. Current in coil 1 sets flux; part of it links coil 2. Mutual inductance M is the flux linkage in coil 2 per ampere in coil 1. M = k√(L₁L₂), where L₁ and L₂ are the self inductances and k is the coupling coefficient, 0 ≤ k ≤ 1. k = 1 means all flux links both coils; k = 0 means no shared flux.

blocks.where: M is mutual inductance in henries (H); L₁ and L₂ are the self inductances of the two coils in henries; k is the coupling coefficient, 0 ≤ k ≤ 1.

blocks.text: In the mutual-inductance transducer, coil 1 is the primary and coil 2 is the secondary. The armature or core moves and changes the air gap under one coil. That changes L₁, L₂ and k. The AC voltage induced in the secondary, e₂ = M·di₁/dt, changes with position; e₂ is the secondary emf in volts and di₁/dt the rate of change of primary current in A/s. A larger gap gives lower M and lower output. Construction uses two coils on a common iron core, with a movable armature or a movable core.

blocks.text: For a simple air gap, L ∝ 1/g. The curve is nonlinear. Sensitivity is dL/dg = -μ₀ A N² / g². The minus sign means L falls as g rises. The magnitude falls as g rises, so the sensor is most sensitive at small gaps. Keep the working gap small and calibrate over the range.
S = dL/dg = - μ₀ A N² / g²
blocks.where: S is sensitivity in henries per metre (H/m); the negative sign shows L falls when g increases; other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: The inductance exists with a steady current too, but a steady current gives no voltage across it (v = L·di/dt), so the read-out needs AC excitation, typically a few kilohertz. The bridge output is then an AC voltage whose amplitude follows displacement; a phase-sensitive demodulator turns its phase into the sign of the movement.

A differential (push-pull) sensor puts a coil on each side of a central armature. Moving the armature by x shortens one gap to g − x and lengthens the other to g + x, so L₁ = μ₀AN²/(g − x) rises while L₂ = μ₀AN²/(g + x) falls. With the two coils as adjacent arms of a half bridge the output is

blocks.where: V<sub>o</sub> is the bridge output in V rms; V<sub>s</sub> the excitation in V rms; x the armature movement and g the centre gap, in the same unit. The result is exactly linear for the ideal gap law, twice as sensitive as one coil, and cancels drifts common to both coils (worked example 2).

items: Displacement: armature movement changes gap; range typically from fractions of a millimetre to a few millimetres.
Thickness: a metal sheet under the core changes the effective gap; thickness or profile can be checked.

Pressure: a diaphragm moves the armature; pressure bends the diaphragm and changes the gap. Variable-reluctance differential pressure transducers, a magnetic diaphragm between two E-core coils, measure airway pressure and flow in lung-function testing.

Breathing: respiratory inductance plethysmography sews insulated wire loops into elastic belts round the chest and abdomen; breathing changes the area each loop encloses and so its self inductance, giving breathing volume without a mouthpiece.
Some syllabi call these variable reluctance transducers or inductive transducers. For a more linear displacement output, see LVDT.

examples.question: A variable reluctance displacement sensor has N = 500 turns, core area A = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m², nominal air gap g = 1.0 mm, and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. Find the inductance at 1.0 mm and at 1.2 mm, and the percentage change.
steps: Convert gap: g₁ = 1.0 mm = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m; g₂ = 1.2 mm = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m.
Use L ≈ μ₀ A N² / g, because the iron reluctance is small compared with the air gap.
Compute numerator: μ₀ A N² = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(2 × 10⁻⁴)(500²) = 6.283 × 10⁻⁵ H·m.
examples.answer: The inductance is 0.06283 H at 1.0 mm and 0.05236 H at 1.2 mm; the gap rise of 20% gives a fall of 16.67%.

examples.question: Two coils like the one in worked example 1 (N = 500, A = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m²) face a central armature, each with a 1.0 mm gap, and form a half bridge excited at 5 V rms. The armature moves 0.1 mm towards coil 1. Find L₁, L₂ and the output. Compare with one coil against a fixed 62.83 mH arm for ±0.1 mm.
steps: Output V<sub>o</sub> = (5/2) × 0.1000 = 0.250 V rms; at −0.1 mm it is 0.250 V rms in antiphase. Equal and opposite: linear.
The single coil gives +0.132 V and −0.119 V: unequal (non-linear) and about half the push-pull output.
examples.answer: L₁ = 69.81 mH, L₂ = 57.12 mH, output 0.250 V rms, the same size either way; one coil gives only +0.132 V and −0.119 V.

traps: Treating L as linear in gap. L ∝ 1/g, so a 20% gap rise gives about 16.7% fall, not 20%.
Using a DC ohmmeter to measure inductance. A coil's resistance is not its inductance; AC excitation and a bridge or meter are needed.
Forgetting the air gap dominates. Iron reluctance is small, but at very small gaps it can matter; do not use L = μ₀AN²/g blindly for a closed core.
Mixing self and mutual inductance. L uses one coil; M uses two coils and k. M = k√(L₁L₂), not L₁ + L₂.
Ignoring sign and direction. L falls as gap rises; a larger gap gives lower output. Phase can indicate direction only in a suitable circuit.

quiz.q: Define magnetic reluctance and give its unit.
quiz.a: Reluctance R is the opposition of a magnetic path to flux: R = l/(μA). Unit: ampere-turns per weber (A·t/Wb) or H⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why does a variable reluctance transducer need AC excitation?
quiz.a: Inductance turns a changing current into a voltage, v = L·di/dt. With a steady current the voltage across the coil is zero, so a gap change cannot be read; AC excitation makes the inductance appear as an impedance ωL that a bridge can measure.

quiz.q: A coil has N = 300 turns, A = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m², g = 0.8 mm. Find L. Use μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
Why does sensitivity fall as the gap rises? Use S = -μ₀AN²/g².
quiz.a: S varies as 1/g², so doubling g cuts sensitivity magnitude to one quarter. The sensor is most sensitive at small gaps.

quiz.q: What is the coupling coefficient k and its range?
quiz.a: k = M/√(L₁L₂), a measure of how strongly the two coils are linked; 0 ≤ k ≤ 1, and k = 1 only when all the flux of each coil links the other.

beyond: Not for the exam. Variable reluctance speed sensors use a toothed wheel and a permanent magnet; the coil voltage pulses as teeth pass, as in car crank and wheel-speed sensors. Search terms: variable reluctance speed sensor, respiratory inductance plethysmography, inductance-to-digital converter.
